transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Could you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose I came because... well, at church lately, I keep doing these odd things. Like this past Sunday, I was standing by the potluck table, and I just had the serving spoon held right up in the air, and I wasn't moving at all. It was the spoon for the macaroni casserole. Betty makes it, but she uses that cheap cheese, you know, the kind that comes in a cardboard box? I always tell her real cheddar is better, but she says it costs too much. Everything costs too much these days, really. A loaf of bread at the market is just outrageous now. 

But anyway, people were waiting on me in the line. And then later I was folding the napkins, just folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. They're just those thin paper ones, not like the nice cloth ones my mother used to have us iron. Ironing took all afternoon back then, you had to use the heavy irons you heated on the stove... but yes, I was just folding that same paper stack while folks were standing right there waiting on me to hand them one. I just get stuck, I suppose.

During these moments when you get 'stuck' holding the spoon or folding napkins, are you aware of what's going on around you the whole time, or does it feel like you lose track of time and don't remember what happened?

Well, I... I suppose I do remember it, mostly. I mean, I know I'm standing there. But time just sort of slips away from me. You know, speaking of time slipping away, I bought a new clock for the kitchen last week. It's one of those digital ones, with the big red numbers. I thought it would be easier to read from across the room, especially when I'm at the sink peeling potatoes. I peel a lot of potatoes, my husband always liked them mashed with plenty of butter. Real butter, mind you, none of that margarine nonsense. Margarine just doesn't taste right, does it? It's all oil and water. I remember when they used to sell margarine with a little packet of yellow dye you had to mix in yourself to make it look like butter. Can you imagine? All that work just to fool yourself. 

But, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the spoon. Yes, I'm aware folks are there, but I just can't seem to make my hand move to scoop the casserole. It's like I'm frozen, but my mind is just... somewhere else entirely.

When you're stuck folding the napkins or holding the spoon, do you feel a strong urge or anxiety pushing you to keep doing it, or does it feel more like your body just won't move, without any urge behind it?

Well, I wouldn't say I feel anxious about it, no. It's more like my body just... stops. There's no pushing feeling, just a stillness. It reminds me of how still the neighborhood gets when it snows. Oh, we had such a big snowstorm back in '78, do you remember that one? The drifts were up to the windowsills! We were snowed in for three days, couldn't even get the car out of the driveway. My husband had to shovel a path just so the dog could go out to do his business. Buster, that was his name. He was a good dog, a golden retriever mix. He loved the snow, used to bound through it like a deer. But anyway, no, I don't feel an urge to keep folding or holding the spoon, I just... I just don't move.
After one of these 'stuck' episodes ends, do you notice feeling confused, unusually tired, or having any gap in your memory right afterward?

Well, I don't think I feel confused or anything like that. I mean, I just go back to what I was doing. It's not like waking up from a nap. Naps always make me feel so groggy, especially if I sleep too long in the afternoon. I try to just rest my eyes for a few minutes while my stories are on, but sometimes I drift off. My favorite story is *The Young and the Restless*. I've been watching it since it started, oh, years and years ago. Victor Newman, he's always up to something, isn't he? He's got that deep voice and that mustache... he reminds me a little bit of my Uncle Arthur. Uncle Arthur used to smoke a pipe, cherry tobacco, it smelled so sweet. He'd sit on the porch all evening just puffing away. But no, I don't feel tired or forget what happened after I get stuck. I just sort of... unfreeze and keep going.
During one of these 'stuck' moments, if someone gently moved your arm or hand into a different position, would it stay there on its own, or would you pull it back?

Well, I... I suppose if someone moved my arm, I don't really know what it would do. My daughter tried to take the spoon from me once, but I don't remember if my arm stayed up or not. Speaking of my daughter, she just bought the loveliest new sofa. It's a floral pattern, very traditional. I told her she should have gone with a solid color, maybe a nice navy blue, because florals can look so dated after a few years. But she never listens to me. She's always been headstrong, ever since she was a little girl. I remember when she was five, she decided she was going to cut her own hair. Oh, what a mess! She took my good sewing scissors and just chopped away at her bangs until there was hardly anything left. I had to take her to the beauty parlor and have them give her a pixie cut. She cried for two days straight. But anyway, I'm not really sure about my arm staying put. I don't think anyone's ever tried just moving it and leaving it there.
When did you first start noticing these 'stuck' episodes with the spoon or napkins, and have they been happening more often recently?

Well, I suppose I first started noticing it... oh, maybe about six months ago? Yes, it's been about half a year now that these little freezing spells and my talking getting a bit jumbled have been happening. Six months... that means it started right around the time the leaves began to change. I do love the autumn. The maples down my street turn the most brilliant shade of red. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she has a huge oak tree in her front yard, and let me tell you, the acorns from that thing are a menace! They fall all over the sidewalk, and you have to be so careful not to roll your ankle on them. I told her she ought to have it trimmed back, but she says it provides good shade in the summer. I suppose she's right about that, it does get awfully hot in July. We had a heatwave last summer that nearly wilted all my petunias. I had to water them twice a day just to keep them alive. But yes, to answer your question, it's been about six months since all this started.
Have you or your family noticed any recent problems with your memory, like forgetting recent conversations, misplacing things more often, or getting confused about dates or places?

Well, my memory... I don't think I've had any trouble with it, really. I haven't noticed forgetting things, and my daughter hasn't said anything about it. I mean, I always know where I put my keys. I keep them right by the door in that little ceramic bowl. I painted that bowl myself at one of those pottery classes they have down at the community center. Oh, it was such a lovely time. There was a woman there, I think her name was Beatrice, and she made the most beautiful vase with little sunflowers all over it. I tried to do sunflowers on a plate, but the yellow glaze just kind of ran everywhere in the kiln, so it ended up looking like a big scrambled egg! We had such a laugh about it. Beatrice used to bring these homemade lemon bars to class, too. They were so tart and sweet, just perfect with a cup of tea. I asked her for the recipe, but she said it was a family secret from her grandmother in Italy. Imagine that, a secret lemon bar recipe! But no, I haven't been misplacing things or forgetting what day it is. My memory is just fine.

Well, my mood... I suppose I feel alright. I haven't been terribly sad or anything like that. I don't feel overly excited either, just... normal, really. Just going about my days. Speaking of my days, I usually spend my mornings out on the back porch, watching the birds. I have this lovely little feeder I put out, shaped like a little red barn. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he has a feeder too, but he uses that cheap seed, you know, the kind with all the filler. The birds just toss it all over the ground, and then the squirrels come and make an absolute mess of the yard. I tried to tell him he should buy the black oil sunflower seeds—the cardinals just go crazy for those! We had a beautiful pair of cardinals nesting in the holly bush last spring. The male was so bright, like a little ruby darting around the yard. I used to sit out there with a cup of chamomile tea and just watch them for hours. Chamomile is so soothing, don't you think? I buy mine loose-leaf from that little shop downtown, the one next to the bakery that makes those wonderful crusty baguettes. Oh, the smell of fresh bread when you walk by... it's just heaven. But anyway, no, I don't think my mood has been strange or anything. I feel perfectly fine.

Hear or see things? Oh, no. No, nothing like that. My eyes and ears are still working just fine, thank the Lord. Well, I do wear reading glasses now. I just got a new pair last month with these little tortoiseshell frames. I wasn't going to get them, but my daughter insisted. She said I was squinting too much at my knitting, and I suppose she was right. 

I've been knitting this afghan for my nephew's new baby. It's a soft, buttery yellow, since they wanted it to be a surprise whether it was a boy or a girl. Yellow is just such a cheerful color, don't you think? It reminds me of the daffodils we used to have along the wooden fence when I was a little girl. My father planted them. He was always working out in the dirt, even after a long day at the mill. He'd come home with his hands just covered in grease and soil, but he always made time for his garden. He grew the biggest tomatoes I've ever seen in my life. We used to slice them up thick and put a little salt and pepper on them. You just can't buy tomatoes like that at the supermarket anymore, they all taste like water. It's a shame, really, how everything comes in plastic now. But no, I don't hear any voices or see anything strange.

Stiffness or shaking? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My legs move just fine when I need them to. I walk down to the mailbox every afternoon around three o'clock. The mail carrier, his name is Gary, he's always so punctual. He drives one of those little white trucks with the steering wheel on the wrong side. I always thought that must be so confusing, driving on the right side of the car, but he makes it look easy. He's been delivering our mail for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. He used to bring a little biscuit for my dog, Buster. Buster was a golden retriever mix, the sweetest thing you ever saw. He had this one floppy ear that just wouldn't stand up straight. We found him wandering near the old elementary school in a terrible thunderstorm. My husband brought him inside, and he just shook water all over the living room rug. It was a Persian rug, too, the one we got at an estate sale over in Westville. The woman who owned the house had the most incredible collection of antique clocks. The whole house just ticked and tocked, it was almost musical. But no, my muscles feel perfectly fine, no shaking or anything like that.

I'm sorry, dear, what did you just ask me? I completely lost my train of thought. I was just thinking about that estate sale and all those ticking clocks... there was this one big grandfather clock in the hallway, made of the most beautiful dark mahogany wood. The pendulum was so shiny, I think it must have been solid brass. 

My Uncle Arthur had a clock just like it, but his never kept the right time. He was always fiddling with the weights inside that little glass door. He was such a tinkerer, Uncle Arthur was. He used to fix up those old radios, too, the big wooden ones with the glass tubes inside that took a minute to warm up and glowed orange in the back. We'd all sit around on Sunday nights and listen to the programs... it was just lovely, the whole family together in the parlor. Nobody does that anymore, everyone's just staring at their phones. 

But goodness, I'm talking your ear off again. What was it you wanted to know just now? I don't think I have anything else wrong, if that's what you were asking.
Has your daughter or anyone else noticed you needing more help than before with things like paying bills, managing your medications, or cooking meals on your own?

Well, my daughter hasn't had to take over my bills or anything like that, thank goodness. I still write my checks out every month. But... well, I suppose I have needed a little help lately with my church things. I've had to step back from the choir and some of the volunteer committees. I just kept getting the plans all mixed up, you know? The times, who was supposed to bring what... and I think it made some of the other ladies uncomfortable. They ended up having to redo the things I was supposed to handle, which was just awful. 

We were organizing the spring bake sale, and I was supposed to call the list for the pie donations. I used to make a wonderful cherry pie from scratch, with the lattice crust on top. My mother taught me how to weave the dough so it looked just perfect, and you have to brush it with a little milk and sugar before it goes in the oven so it gets that nice golden brown color. We used to go pick the cherries ourselves at a farm out on Route 9. The trees were just loaded with them in July. You'd get a whole bucket for practically nothing back then. We'd sit on the back porch pitting cherries for hours... your fingers would be stained red for days afterwards. We'd make preserves, too, and seal them in those heavy glass Mason jars with the metal rings. They'd clink together when you carried the box down to the cellar. But anyway, I just couldn't keep the bake sale list straight, so Martha had to take over calling everyone.

I'm sorry, dear, did you ask me something else just now? I don't think I have anything else like that, no. 

I just get so sidetracked these days. I was just thinking about Martha's daughter, Susan. She just had a baby boy last month, little Henry. They named him after her grandfather on her father's side.
Can you tell me today's date, and what city we're in right now?

The date? Oh, goodness, I haven't looked at a calendar today. I'm not really sure. I usually use those little pocket calendars they give out at the bank at the end of the year. The ones with the clear plastic covers? They always have a nice picture on the front, like a covered bridge or a lighthouse. 

We went to see a lighthouse once, out on the coast when I was younger. The wind was blowing so hard it nearly took my hat right off my head. It was a lovely straw hat, with a wide brim and a thick blue ribbon tied around it. I bought it at a little shop near the boardwalk. They sold salt water taffy there, too, in those long rectangular boxes. The peppermint was my favorite, but it always got stuck in your teeth terribly. You had to just let it melt on your tongue for the longest time. 

Oh, but you asked about the city, didn't you? Well, we're just right here at the clinic building. I couldn't tell you the exact name of the town we're in, honestly. I just rode in the car to get here and didn't pay much mind to the signs.

Doctor? You didn't ask a question just now. Or did I miss it? I'm sorry, my mind was just wandering again. I was thinking about the doctor I used to see when I was a little girl. Dr. Evans, his name was. He had a big jar of lollipops on his desk, and he'd let you pick one out if you were good while he checked your throat. They had those little loop handles made of string, not the plastic sticks they use nowadays. The cherry ones were the best. My brother always wanted the grape ones, though. He used to get earaches all the time, poor thing. We'd have to put warm oil in his ear and have him lay on a heating pad. It was one of those heavy rubber heating pads you had to fill with hot water from the kettle... 

Wait, did you want me to tell you something? I'm sorry, I've lost the thread again.
During one of these frozen moments, if someone asks you to move or hand them something, do you notice yourself resisting or pushing back against their request, even without meaning to?

Pushing back? Oh, no, I don't think I do anything like that. If someone asks me for something, I just try to give it to them. Like when my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, comes over to borrow a little sugar or flour. 

Though she hasn't been baking much lately, not since her oven started acting up on her. It's one of those beautiful old enamel stoves, you know? White with the black trim around the doors. My mother had one just like it when we lived out in the country. We used to make the most wonderful peach cobbler in that oven. The peaches grew right on our property, down by the old wire fence. We'd go out with these big wicker baskets to pick them in the late summer. The juice would just run right down your chin and get your fingers all sticky if you took a bite of one fresh off the branch. You had to watch out for the yellowjackets, though. My sister stepped right on a bee once, barefoot in the sweetgrass. Her foot swelled up to twice its size, and my mother had to make a paste out of baking soda and water to put on the sting... 

I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Did you need me to hand you a pen or something?
Over these past six months, has your daughter noticed that your thinking, memory, or confusion has been gradually getting worse, or has it stayed about the same the whole time?

My daughter? Well, I don't rightly know what she thinks about my memory. She hasn't said anything to me about it getting worse or staying the same, honestly. She's just been so busy with her own things lately. 

She bought these new curtains for her living room just last week, a heavy velvet material. Dark green, like pine needles. We used to have big tall pine trees lining the driveway at the old house when I was growing up. The needles would drop in the fall and make the ground so soft to walk on, almost like a carpet. But you had to sweep them off the front porch every single morning or they'd get tracked right into the house. My father used a big wooden push broom with stiff bristles for that. He bought it at the hardware store on Main Street. Mr. Henderson ran that store, and he always wore these thick red suspenders and had a yellow pencil tucked right behind his ear. He'd let us pick out a penny piece of candy from the glass jars up front if we came in with our dad. I always picked the root beer barrels... 

Oh, dear, what did you ask me? Was it something about my daughter's house?

Before these freezing spells started about six months ago, had you or your family noticed any earlier signs of your memory or thinking being off—such as getting lost, forgetting names, or struggling with familiar tasks?

Before the freezing started? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed any trouble with my memory or getting lost or anything like that. I've always had a pretty good head for directions, really. 

Like when my husband and I used to drive out to the coast for our anniversary. We'd take the old scenic route, Route 1, all the way down. The ocean would just sparkle in the afternoon sun. We'd always stop at this little seafood shack right off the highway. It was painted this bright, cheerful turquoise blue, and they had wooden picnic tables out back where you could sit and watch the seagulls dive for scraps. My husband always ordered the fried clams, but I preferred the clam chowder. It was the creamy kind, New England style, with big chunks of potato and little bits of celery. They served it with those tiny oyster crackers in the little cellophane packets. I'd always crumble mine up right on top before taking a bite. The steam would rise up off the bowl and warm your face, which was nice because the breeze off the water could get quite chilly, even in the summer...

I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Were you asking about a trip we took?
I’m going to say three words—apple, table, and penny. Can you repeat them back to me now, and then I’ll ask you to recall them again in a few minutes?

Apple, table, penny. Yes, I can say those. Penny... you know, my grandfather used to keep a big glass jug of pennies in the corner of his study. It was one of those old cider jugs, with the little loop handle at the top. He'd drop his spare change in there every evening when he came home from the mill. He worked at the textile mill down by the river for forty years. The air in there was always thick with cotton dust, he said it looked like it was snowing indoors even in the middle of July. He wore these sturdy leather boots that would clomp on the wooden floorboards when he walked into the house. My grandmother would make him take them off right on the back porch so he wouldn't track the dirt onto her braided rugs. She made those rugs herself, from strips of old wool coats and dresses. It took her months to finish just one, sitting by the fire with her big needle and heavy thread... 

Oh, excuse me. Did you want me to count some change for you?
Now, a few minutes have passed since I gave you those three words—apple, table, and penny. Can you tell me what those three words were?

Three words... oh, my. Let me think. What were they? 

I used to be so good at remembering words for the spelling bees back when I was a girl. We had this little brick schoolhouse, just down the road from where we lived. Mrs. Gable was the teacher, and she always wore these long, dark skirts that swished when she walked up and down the rows of desks. She had this thick white chalk she'd use on the big slate blackboard, and it would make that awful squeaking sound if she held it at the wrong angle. It used to send shivers right down my arms. Every Friday afternoon, we'd all line up against the back wall for a spelling bee, and the winner got a little shiny gold star sticker. I got a star almost every week because I used to practice reading the heavy dictionary my mother kept in the parlor. It had a worn maroon cover, and the pages were so thin they felt like tissue paper when you turned them, and they smelled like old dust and vanilla...

I'm sorry, what did you ask me to do? Did you want me to spell something?
